A genuine Rekor v2 entry whose verifier is a certificate — the v3 shape,
complete, and verifiable end to end.

Published 2026-08-16 to https://log2025-1.rekor.sigstore.dev (HTTP 201
Created, logIndex 67766084) and read back out of the log's own static tiles
on the same day. Nothing in this repository authored the log's half of any of
it: not the checkpoint, not its signature lines, not the tree the audit path
walks.

  statement.json           470 B  the in-toto Statement, byte-exact — the
                                  DSSE PAE preimage the leaf's digest commits
                                  to. Preserved this time, which is what makes
                                  the fixture total (see "what this proves").
  certificate.der          944 B  the entry's verifier, extracted from
                                  spec.hashedRekordV002.signature.verifier
                                    .x509Certificate.rawBytes.
  canonicalized_body.json 1631 B  the Merkle leaf preimage, verbatim, as the
                                  log returned it.
  checkpoint.txt           643 B  the signed note at tree size 67 766 085.
                                  It carries FOUR signature lines: the log's
                                  own Ed25519 signature plus three witness
                                  cosignatures. This design does not interpret
                                  cosignatures at all, but the parser has to
                                  tolerate them — narrowing it to a single
                                  signature would reject every checkpoint the
                                  production log serves, and this file is the
                                  regression test for that.
  proof.bin               3050 B  the encoded RekorProof v3 record — the
                                  exact bytes a zone serves at
                                  _synchronicity-rekor.<apex>, carrying 8
                                  audit-path hashes. The tests decode this
                                  through the client's own reader rather than
                                  reassembling the record field by field.
  log_index.txt                   67766084.
  anchor.txt               144 B  the DNSSEC trust anchor this zone is under,
                                  in --dnssec-anchor syntax.

The certificate is the shape §2 specifies: self-signed P-256, CN
"synchronicity zone key", basicConstraints CA:FALSE critical, keyUsage
digitalSignature critical, one dNSName SAN
`zone-key-transparency.demo.invalid`, and **both custom extensions** — the
DNSSEC chain under 2.25.1555716359 and the succession countersignature under
2.25.1138370866, the narrowed OIDs from §2.2.

Those extensions are why this fixture exists in its current form. An earlier
version of this design used full 128-bit UUID arcs, and the log refused every
certificate carrying them with an opaque `400 invalid hashedrekord request` —
Go's encoding/asn1 rejects OID components that overflow int32, so Rekor's
parser failed before it ever reached the extension. No local test could see
it: OpenSSL and Erlang's public_key both parse the wide form happily. The
201 above, at 944 bytes with both extensions present, is the empirical answer
to both questions that raised — the arcs are acceptable and the size is fine.


What this fixture proves, in tests/rekor_zone_key.rs::real_rekor_v3
-------------------------------------------------------------------

It is **total**: `rekor::verify` — the actual client verifier, no test
double — runs to a successful VerifiedRecord over these bytes:

  - the served proof record decodes through the client's wire reader;
  - the log id matches a key in the *embedded* Sigstore pin set;
  - the checkpoint verifies under that key, with the log's own signature
    found among the four lines the note carries;
  - the leaf is SHA-256(0x00 || canonicalized_body) and the RFC 6962 walk
    over 8 audit-path hashes reaches the checkpoint's root, in a real tree of
    67.7 million entries;
  - the body parses as hashedrekord 0.0.2 with an x509Certificate verifier;
  - the certificate parses, its single dNSName SAN is the apex, and its
    SubjectPublicKeyInfo is the zone key;
  - signature.content verifies under that key with the entry's data.digest as
    the prehashed message (independently confirmed with
    `openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey pub.pem -sigfile sig.der
     -in digest.bin -pkeyopt digest:sha256` → Signature Verified
    Successfully). Because that digest *is* SHA-256(PAE), the same signature
    verifies as ECDSA-SHA256 over the PAE, which is how ring is asked;
  - data.digest is SHA-256 of the DSSE PAE of statement.json;
  - the Statement round-trips through this build's canonical renderer byte
    for byte, and binds the apex, key tag, flags, algorithm and DNSKEY digest;
  - the carried DNSSEC chain validates against the anchor in anchor.txt;
  - the result is action `rollover`, log_index 67766084, tree_size 67766085,
    origin log2025-1.rekor.sigstore.dev.

With teeth: the same proof offered for a different key, and for a different
apex, is refused as a binding failure; and one flipped byte in the body
leaves the leaf outside the tree.

crates/synch-monitor/tests/real_entry.rs classifies the very same bytes, so
one fixture covers both halves of the invariant — the client accepts it, and
the monitor does not put it in the silent bin.


What it does not prove, stated plainly
--------------------------------------

**The chain is self-anchored.** We own no DNSSEC-signed domain, so the chain
inside this certificate terminates at the apex itself rather than climbing to
the ICANN root: `zone-key-transparency.demo.invalid` is its own trust anchor,
which is why anchor.txt ships beside it and why the tests pass that anchor in
exactly as a `--dnssec-anchor` operator would. **A public monitor rooted at
ICANN files this entry tier C** — correctly, since nothing outside that
private universe can tell whether the key was ever delegated. Real-world,
ICANN-rooted chain validation is anchored separately by
tests/fixtures/dnssec_chain, a live `cloudflare.com` delegation with a
two-level DS ladder, RSASHA256 at the root and ECDSAP256SHA256 below it. This
fixture is about interoperating with the log; that one is about interoperating
with the DNS.

**It is a rollover whose predecessor key was not retained.** The succession
extension names key tag 56306 and the countersignature is real and verifies,
but the private half was discarded after publication. So a monitor that has
not been told about that predecessor classifies this entry **tier B** — which
is the correct and expected answer for an uncountersigned-looking rotation,
and is asserted as such. The monitor suite also seeds the predecessor's SPKI
out of the extension itself to exercise the tier A path over the same real
bytes.

The demo apex is under `.invalid` (RFC 2606), so it can never resolve and
cannot be mistaken for a live deployment.

Regenerating: this cannot be regenerated from the repository — it is a
permanent public record. Re-publishing would mint a new entry at a new index,
which is the point of an append-only log. If the certificate's shape ever
changes, submit one entry by hand, read the status code before trusting any
local test, and replace this whole directory together with its index.
